subject: LLM private-deploy: operational impact of peering vs endpoint vs S2S (checklist + PoC asks)

Jonas / Kim —

Thanks again for the architecture session yesterday. We walked away with three competing paths for connectivity to our private deployment: VPC peering (cross-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a managed site-to-site VPN to our colo. Before we start a PoC we need two things from Redwood so the infra/security teams can sign off: a concise operational-impact checklist (what we must run, what breaks under each failure mode) and a short set of baseline performance expectations (latency, bandwidth, expected packet loss) per option.

Specific asks:
- Short checklist for runbooks and required IAM/network primitives for each option (peering, PrivateLink, S2S)
- CIDR overlap handling and recommended CIDR ranges that avoid rework
- Observability mappings (what logs/metrics we expect, how to trace request flows)
- Estimated cost buckets (data egress, per-endpoint charges, GW appliance cost)
- PoC proposal: minimal config to validate throughput and failover (suggested test plan + time box)

We have a compliance window: need sign-off on the connectivity approach by Dec 10 so procurement can start the SOW approvals. Can you return a single doc + a short email summary with the quick rec?

— Sara
Director, Cloud Architecture
Halcyon Financial

Subject: Re: LLM private-deploy: operational impact of peering vs endpoint vs S2S (checklist + PoC asks)

Sara —

Attached is the matrix you have and a one-pager summary below. We kept the checklist pragmatic so your security and NetOps teams can map it straight into their runbooks. High-level guidance first, then a short PoC plan at the bottom.

Quick recommendation (summary):
- Control-plane and metadata: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) gives the tightest least-privilege boundary and reduces blast radius for API/control traffic.
- Bulk data (high-throughput inference payloads): VPC peering when CIDR and cross-account limitations allow — it's simplest for high-throughput, low-latency flows and supports native path MTU, but beware transitive limitations and cross-region caveats.
- Fallback/remote sites: Site-to-site VPN is a reasonable fallback for remote colo or legacy networks where peering or endpoint deployment is infeasible; expect higher latency and additional operational overhead.

Operational checklist highlights (one-liners you can drop into runbooks):
- Peering: verify non-overlapping CIDRs; update route tables in both accounts; add specific security group rules to restrict access to Redwood model subnets; enable VPC Flow Logs and mirror to your SIEM; test asymmetric routing by forcing IPs through peering and validating stateful firewall rules.
- PrivateLink: provision interface endpoints in your consumer VPCs; ensure ENI quotas are available (for high-scale, request multiple quotas in advance); configure SGs on the endpoint ENIs to restrict source subnets; add endpoint-specific DNS entries (we provide a private zone mapping); monitor ENI creation failures and ENI-level metrics.
- Site-to-site VPN: pre-provision customer gateway, configure Phase 1/2 ciphers per your policy; include MTU/MSS adjustments; run iperf and TCP-based tests for throughput; plan for HA (two tunnels across distinct endpoints).

Failure-mode mapping (short):
- Peering: failure = route table misconfig / peering detached -> traffic drops silently (easy to detect via VPC Flow Logs but needs runbook to rollback).
- PrivateLink: failure = ENI limit or endpoint DNS misconfiguration -> control-plane traffic fails but dataplane (peering) unaffected. Endpoint failures are obvious in ENI/Endpoint metrics; you can auto-failover to peering if both are configured.
- S2S VPN: failure = cipher or tunnel flapping -> intermittent latency/packet loss and TCP retransmits; requires BGP/route convergence watch and monitoring of tunnels.

Observability & tracing: all options should integrate with: VPC Flow Logs, Redwood request-level tracing (we inject a trace-id header and surface it in our Console), CloudWatch/Network Device SNMP. For PrivateLink we also surface endpoint ENI metrics and per-ENI error counters.

Cost buckets (approx):
- Peering: minimal per-hour costs; watch for cross-AZ or cross-region data egress charges.
- PrivateLink: per-endpoint hourly + per-GB processed model; can be cost-effective for low-rate control-plane traffic but grows with many endpoints.
- S2S VPN: per-hour tunnel pricing + egress; appliance costs if you go with managed NGFW.

PoC proposal (2-week, two-step):
1) Week A — minimal connectivity test (non-prod):
   - Option A: set up VPC peering between Halcyon non-prod VPC and Redwood sandbox; run 1Gbps iperf TCP tests, measure 99th/50th percentile latency for 256B/4KB/16KB payloads, run long-tail token generation (10K requests) to surface tail latencies.
   - Option B: provision a PrivateLink endpoint for control-plane; validate auth, DNS, and connection tracking.
   - Deliverable: perf report + runbook fragments.
2) Week B — resilience + scale test:
   - Bring up an S2S VPN as a simulated remote site; run failover scenarios (bring down peering, test PrivateLink-only control traffic, force asymmetric routes) and run smoke tests for application-level correctness.
   - Deliverable: go/no-go recommendation for production connectivity and a short list of required quota requests/infra changes.

I'll attach the matrix and a diagram for the PrivateLink pattern. We can also provide a scoped SOW for the PoC if you want Redwood to do engineering time.

Next steps: if this looks good I can turn the one-pager into a PDF for your procurement and schedule a 30m NetOps walkthrough next week.

— Jonas

Sara —

A couple of operational constraints from NetOps/Security I wanted to call out specifically (so the PoC plan can avoid surprises):

1) CIDR hygiene: Halcyon's prod VPCs use /16 blocks across several accounts. For peering we need at least /20 contiguous ranges for our subnets to avoid NATting. If you have existing /16s, we should isolate a /20 for Redwood traffic (we can document the blocks).

2) ENI quotas and cold-starts: PrivateLink traffic creates an ENI per AZ per endpoint. If you scale quickly through traffic spikes you will hit ENI quotas first. Please request ENI quota increases before Week A if you expect bursty load.

3) TLS termination & KMS: For S2S we recommend TLS termination at your perimeter if you have HSM/KMS controls there. For PrivateLink/peering we rely on in-flight AES-256 with optional application layer encryption. We'll provide key rotation guidance.

4) Monitoring playbook: enable VPC Flow Logs to a centralized S3 + lifecycle policy, forward critical alerts to your PagerDuty channel (we'll provide CloudWatch metric thresholds).

Attached is a redlined PoC test-plan template and a short SOW stub for procurement.

— Kim
Director, Solutions Engineering, Redwood Inference

Team —

Great detail here, thank you. HalcyonNetOps reviewed the checklist and we have an internal preference:

- Use PrivateLink for all control-plane and admin APIs (we prefer non-routable, ENI-based endpoints for least privilege).
- For inference payloads we are split; performance team wants peering for predictable low-latency, but procurement is wary of cross-account CIDR changes.

Decision for PoC: proceed with Jonas' two-step plan. Immediate actions on our side:
- We will carve a /20 in our non-prod account (expected by Tue 23 Nov).
- Request ENI quota bump for the AZs in non-prod (we'll notify you when approved).
- We want Redwood to own the Week A perf runs and provide the perf report. Please include the iperf configs and the trace-id correlation in the report.

Can you confirm costs for Redwood-managed PoC time (est. 2 engineer-days) so procurement can issue a small MSA addendum? If you can, please send a short SOW and ballpark cost.

— Marco
Head of Infrastructure, Halcyon Financial
